assistant_message.content: I’ll identify the product from the listing and verify its intended use and evidence-based benefits.
I’ll now inspect the product page and cross-check its listing details against independent information.

The item is advertised as a portable “32 TB” external SSD, but the price and third-party reports raise strong authenticity concerns. I’ll verify the warning signs before giving you a practical recommendation.

This is advertised as a **portable external solid-state drive (SSD)** claiming **32 TB of storage** and extremely high transfer speeds. A genuine device of that type would be used to store and move large files—such as photo libraries, video projects, computer backups, game files, and 4K movies—without relying on cloud storage. The legitimate benefits of a real portable SSD are convenience, compact size, fast file transfers, and offline backup capacity.

However, the benefits advertised here are **not credible for this specific product**. The listing offers a supposed 32 TB “German pro SSD” for about **$54**, with vague or inconsistent specifications and dramatic claims such as transferring three 4K movies in one second. That is an extreme mismatch between the claimed capacity/performance and the price. [The product page](https://usbest1.com/products/16075014289626958844931170) does not identify a recognizable drive manufacturer or provide the detailed technical specifications you would expect for genuine high-capacity storage.

More importantly, the Better Business Bureau’s Scam Tracker has a report tied to this **exact product URL**. The reporter said all three drives received were unusable and identified the item as counterfeit or materially different from the listing; BBB categorizes the report as a **Counterfeit Product** report. That is a consumer report rather than a formal finding, but it is a serious, directly relevant warning. [BBB Scam Tracker report](https://www.bbb.org/scamtracker/lookupscam/1402327?returnTo=%2Fscamtracker%2Flookupscam%3Fview%3Dmap)

I would **not buy it** or trust it with anything important. Fake-capacity drives can tell the computer that they have, for example, 32 TB available while containing only a small amount of real flash storage. They may appear to accept files, then silently discard or overwrite data after their real capacity is exceeded. Gibson Research explains this failure mode and provides a free capacity-checking utility, [ValiDrive](https://www.grc.com/validrive.htm), which writes and reads random test data across a USB drive’s declared space.

If you already received one, do not put your only copies of files on it. Photograph the listing and packaging, preserve order/payment records, test it only when it contains no valuable data, and promptly use your card or payment provider’s dispute process if it fails the capacity test.
